title: Enabling Evolutionary Architecture Through the Preservation of Change Locality
gist: An InfoQ Certified Architect Program capstone argues that evolutionary architecture should be measured not by whether a system can change but by whether the team receiving a request can make it with proportional context — a property the authors call change locality. Using an e-commerce address-change case and a digital retail bank account-opening case, they diagnose 'boundary drift' (decision authority migrates while org and system structure stay put), name disproportionate cognitive load as the leading indicator, and prescribe a three-move intervention: redistribute repeated mechanics to platforms, expose essential policy across boundaries, and rehearse real exception paths.

themes.theme: Change Locality as the Evolvability Test

insights.claim: Evolutionary architecture should be judged by a concrete team-level test — whether the team owning a business capability can answer 'what can change here', 'what contract protects neighboring work', and 'what evidence proves the change is safe' without reconstructing the whole system — rather than by whether the system is theoretically changeable.
insights.speaker: Michael Fischer
insights.so_what: Gives a cheap, observable diagnostic for engineering-org health: teams that cannot answer all three questions for their own capability are carrying hidden delivery drag that will show up as slipping roadmaps before it shows up in any metric.
insights.quote: A business capability has locality when the team responsible for it can answer three questions without reconstructing the whole system:

insights.claim: At sufficient scale almost any software system can be made to change, so changeability is not the scarce resource — coherent change is, meaning the ability of one team to evolve a capability without reconstructing the whole system each time.
insights.speaker: Michael Fischer
insights.so_what: Reframes 'modernization' spend: rewrites that improve technical malleability without fixing who owns which decision will not improve delivery throughput, which is the ROI most transformation budgets are sold on.
insights.quote: The architectural question is not only, "Can the system change?" It is, "Can the right team make the change with the right amount of context?"

insights.claim: Change locality is a proportionality property, not isolation: required understanding should scale with the scope of the change, so needing cross-team coordination is acceptable when the change genuinely spans domains but not when a copy edit forces a team to learn the whole delivery model.
insights.speaker: Michael Fischer
insights.so_what: Cuts against the reflex to split services further; the useful intervention is often making coordination explicit rather than eliminating it, which changes what platform and tooling budgets should actually buy.
insights.quote: the understanding required to make a change should be proportional to the scope of the change

insights.claim: Architectural boundaries are best modeled as provisional hypotheses about which decisions should change together, drawn against a snapshot of the business, and they predictably decay through four mechanisms: products expanding into adjacent capabilities, teams splitting or merging, platforms absorbing responsibilities from product teams, and supporting or outsourced capabilities becoming core.
insights.speaker: Michael Fischer
insights.so_what: Provides a checklist for when to re-audit architecture: any of these four corporate events (M&A, reorg, platform consolidation, insourcing) is a leading indicator that delivery cost is about to rise even with no code change.
insights.quote: Boundaries are hypotheses about which decisions or components should change together.

insights.claim: Boundary drift is defined as the gap between the boundaries a system still expresses and the boundaries the pending change actually requires — the decisions move while the structure stays fixed.
insights.speaker: Michael Fischer
insights.so_what: Names a failure mode that org charts and service catalogs cannot detect, since both look unchanged; the only observable is rising coordination cost per unit of change.
insights.quote: the decisions have moved/changed; the structure has not
insights.locator: The gap between the boundaries that the system still expresses

insights.claim: In the e-commerce case, a seemingly trivial request to let customers change a delivery address after ordering turned out to depend on warehouse cutoff times, fraud rules, delivery partner instructions, support scripts, notification templates and refund policy — so the checkout team owned the request but not the decisions determining whether the change was safe.
insights.speaker: Michael Fischer
insights.so_what: Concrete template for estimating risk on 'small' feature requests: check whether decision authority for the safety constraints sits inside the requesting team before sizing the work.
insights.quote: This most recent request looked small: let customers change a delivery address after placing an order.

insights.claim: Drift accumulates through individually reasonable business learnings — some items leaving the warehouse quickly, some addresses triggering fraud checks, some delivery partners needing earlier instructions, premium customers getting more flexible service, support handling phone exceptions — that collectively redefine what an address update means at different fulfillment stages.
insights.speaker: Michael Fischer
insights.so_what: Explains why no single decision looks wrong in retrospect and why drift is never caught by change review: the damage is only visible in aggregate, so it needs periodic structural audit rather than per-change gating.
insights.quote: Each change is reasonable. Together, they change what an address update means at different stages of order fulfillment.

insights.claim: In a digital retail bank case, growth from a single savings product into loans with automated underwriting, checking accounts requiring debit card printing and mailing, and expanding compliance rules pushed flagged applications into document-request workflows that stretched decision time from minutes into days — while the onboarding team still owned the application form and received change requests directly.
insights.speaker: Michael Fischer
insights.so_what: Shows drift is worse in regulated growth: every new product line adds a decision owner outside the customer-facing team, so fintech scaling stories should be stress-tested on onboarding-time regressions, not just product count.
insights.quote: The boundary never moved on paper. The path of change did.
insights.locator: We can also consider a software engineering team at a digital retail bank

themes.theme: Cognitive Load as the Leading Indicator

insights.claim: The diagnostic signal of broken change locality is not the number of teams involved in a change but the requesting team's inability to tell which decisions matter, who owns them, and what evidence would prove the change safe.
insights.speaker: Michael Fischer
insights.so_what: Corrects a common measurement error — dependency counts and team-touch counts are poor proxies; the sharper question to ask a team is whether they can name the decision owners.
insights.quote: the signal is not "five teams are involved." The signal is that checkout cannot tell which decisions matter, who owns them, or what evidence proves the change is safe.

insights.claim: Four observable symptoms indicate the boundary model no longer matches the structure of change: a modest feature that turns out to touch three systems with unclear ownership, an incident post-mortem where recovery depended on one engineer's memory of a non-obvious dependency, onboarding taking months because safety-critical knowledge is not in code, tests, docs or dashboards, and a 10-line pull request generating a fifty-comment review thread.
insights.speaker: Michael Fischer
insights.so_what: These are all measurable from existing telemetry (PR comment ratios, ramp time, estimate variance), making boundary drift trackable as an operational metric rather than a subjective architecture opinion.
insights.quote: A 10-line pull request generates a fifty-comment review thread because reviewers cannot agree which behavior is correct.
insights.locator: The same signal appears outside this example

themes.theme: Sociotechnical Causes: Technology, Teams, Process, People

insights.claim: Shared platforms cause drift when they remove duplication but hide decisions: a shipping platform that centralizes carrier rules, warehouse cutoffs and delivery promises may be the right trade-off, yet the consuming team still needs to know whether 'too late to change' means packed, dispatched, fraud-locked, partner-notified or refund-sensitive.
insights.speaker: Michael Fischer
insights.so_what: Direct warning for internal-platform and IDP investment theses: consolidation that abstracts away decision semantics buys duplication savings while transferring an unpriced comprehension cost onto product teams.
insights.quote: When shared platforms remove duplication but hide decisions, this can be a symptom of technology drift.

insights.claim: Ownership lines that each make sense locally — checkout owning customer experience, warehouse owning physical fulfillment, fraud owning risk, support owning exceptions — can leave no team owning the end-to-end policy that the business actually needs to evolve.
insights.speaker: Michael Fischer
insights.so_what: The gap to hunt for in any org review is the unowned end-to-end policy, which appears in no team's charter and therefore in no team's budget or backlog.
insights.quote: In this example, no team clearly owns the end-to-end policy.

insights.claim: Process artifacts accumulate as fossilized learning that outlives the operating model that produced them: a review step added after a delivery incident, support scripts that quietly become the practical source of exception policy, and refund approvals sitting in a separate workflow all preserve an older model of the product.
insights.speaker: Michael Fischer
insights.so_what: Support scripts as de facto policy is the most overlooked instance — it means customer-facing promises are being set outside engineering's change control entirely.
insights.quote: Support scripts may have become the practical source of exception policy.

insights.claim: When experienced engineers, operations leads and support managers are the only reliable memory of why certain promises are unsafe, the system can look decoupled in its deployment topology while remaining tightly coupled through the tacit knowledge required to reason about it safely.
insights.speaker: Michael Fischer
insights.so_what: Microservice counts and deployment independence metrics can be entirely satisfied by a system with severe key-person coupling — a real risk for acquirers doing technical diligence on architecture claims.
insights.quote: The risk is that relationships and recollection become the only reliable integration layer.

insights.claim: Redistribution should move repeated mechanics — cutoff calculations, partner status checks, notification delivery, deployment pipelines, infrastructure setup, compliance scaffolding, observability wiring — to a platform or shared service, but must not by default move business policy there, since domain teams need to retain authority over customer promises.
insights.speaker: Michael Fischer
insights.so_what: A clean line for scoping internal platform mandates: mechanics and toil are in scope, customer-promise policy is not — platform teams that cross that line create the very drift they were funded to remove.
insights.quote: The platform can own mechanics and toil; product and domain teams still need clear authority over customer promises.

insights.claim: Exposure means making the constraints that govern safe change legible across boundaries — when an order is packed, when fraud can block an address, when a partner needs final instructions, what support can promise — delivered through explicit ownership, API contracts, contract tests, architecture decision records, service catalogs, meaningful events, dashboards or escalation paths.
insights.speaker: Michael Fischer
insights.so_what: Names the concrete tool categories that address drift (catalogs, contract testing, ADR tooling, event platforms), which is where budget flows once cognitive load is accepted as the bottleneck.
insights.quote: The goal is to make the decisions that govern safe change legible to the teams responsible for evolving the capability.

insights.claim: The pass/fail test for a boundary redesign is rehearsal of the exception paths that previously required expert coordination — can support resolve a known address-change exception from visible policy, can checkout adjust a premium-customer window within guardrails, can the team see when a partner handoff makes the change unsafe — and if every realistic exception still routes to the same experts, locality has not been restored.
insights.speaker: Michael Fischer
insights.so_what: Supplies the missing verification step most re-architectures skip; without it, teams declare victory on structure while the human dependency graph is unchanged.
insights.quote: If every realistic exception still depends on the same experts, locality has not been restored.

themes.theme: Limits: When Not to Optimize for Locality

insights.claim: Reduced cognitive load is not automatically a win — standardization can improve flow while moving too much decision-making away from the teams closest to the domain, and hiding the wrong complexity produces a low-load team that makes unsafe changes.
insights.speaker: Michael Fischer
insights.so_what: Pushes back on developer-experience pitches sold purely on load reduction; the question to ask is which complexity was hidden, not how much.
insights.quote: Low cognitive load is not valuable if the wrong complexity has been hidden.

insights.claim: Some changes are genuinely cross-cutting — shipping promises, fraud controls, refunds, safety, financial reporting and customer communication — and because the business consequence is shared, these should be coordinated explicitly rather than forced back into a single team's boundary.
insights.speaker: Michael Fischer
insights.so_what: Sets the boundary of the whole thesis: in risk- and consistency-dominated domains (payments, safety, reporting) coordination cost is the correct cost, and autonomy-maximizing architecture is the wrong optimization.
insights.quote: Do not optimize for locality when consistency or risk control matters more than local speed.

insights.claim: No structural style or modeling practice guarantees change locality indefinitely, so boundaries must be treated as living hypotheses that are periodically re-tested against delivery friction, incidents, support escalations, review queues and expert dependency.
insights.speaker: Michael Fischer
insights.so_what: Implies architecture review is a recurring operational function, not a one-time design event — the buyers for drift-detection tooling are permanent rather than project-based.
insights.quote: When even simple changes become negotiations with the entire system, boundary drift has become the dominant cost of changing that capability.
